questions.text: What does ampacity mean in the checked PEC conductor provisions?

options.text: The current a conductor can carry continuously under its use conditions without exceeding its temperature rating.
The physical color of the insulation only.
The number of outlets on a branch circuit only.
The billing demand of the utility service only.

questions.rationale: PEC defines ampacity by continuous current, use conditions, and temperature rating.
questions.explanation: Confuses the temperature ratings and incorrectly suggests THWN requires conduit like THHN does. Reverses the temperature ratings and wet/dry characteristics of both wire types. Suggests the wires are identical, which overlooks critical differences in construction and application. THWN is water-resistant and rated 75°C wet/90°C dry, making it suitable for both wet and dry locations. THHN is a single-conductor wire rated 90°C dry locations only, typically used in conduit systems. THWN's water-resistant nylon coating allows flexible wet/dry use; THHN's design requires conduit protection.
questions.code_citation: PEC Table 310.15(B)(16); Article on Wire Insulation Types and Ratings

questions.text: Which conductor type is source-safe for wet locations under the checked PEC list?

options.text: THWN.
A conductor with no listed wet-location rating.
A bare conductor used as an uninsulated phase conductor.
A decorative cord with no Code type marking.

questions.rationale: THWN appears in the checked PEC wet-location list.
questions.explanation: EMT requires corrosion protection (e.g., PVC coating) for wet locations per PEC. TW is lower-rated (60°C); while acceptable, it's unnecessarily conservative for the application. THHN is single-conductor and requires separate conduit anyway; temperature rating doesn't prevent water ingress. For wet basements, THWN wire's 75°C wet rating and PVC conduit's corrosion resistance combine to provide safe, durable performance in Philippine tropical humidity. Both are rated for wet locations per PEC. Wet locations require combination of wet-rated wire insulation and corrosion-resistant conduit (PVC or IMC).

questions.explanation: NM is restricted to dry residential locations; completely unsuitable for hospitals' critical infrastructure. AC cable lacks the fire-rating properties needed; mechanical protection ≠ fire resistance. While MC provides grounding and some protection, it lacks MI's fire-rated insulation (only 60–90°C, not 250°C). MI cable's mineral insulation (MgO) and copper/steel sheath provide unmatched fire resistance and temperature ratings (250°C dry, 150°C wet). MI cable is suitable for hospital life-safety systems requiring circuit integrity during fire per PEC. PEC recognizes MI as the premium choice for critical circuits. Life-safety and fire-rated circuits require MI cable's mineral insulation, not standard copper insulation.

questions.text: A contractor specifies XHHW wire for the main feeder of an office building. What is the primary advantage of XHHW over THWN for this application?

options.text: XHHW is cheaper and lighter, reducing installation labor costs and overall project expenses.
XHHW has cross-linked polyethylene insulation offering superior thermal stability and durability for high-load applications
XHHW can be installed without conduit, unlike THWN which requires a raceway, simplifying installation.
XHHW can carry 25% more current than THWN at the same wire size due to better heat dissipation, enhancing efficiency.

questions.rationale: XHHW uses cross-linked polyethylene insulation, providing superior durability and thermal stability compared to THWN's thermoplastic coating. This makes XHHW preferred for main feeders and high-load circuits that generate sustained heat. [A]: Incorrectly suggests cost and weight advantages, when XHHW is actually more expensive than THWN. [C]: Confuses installation method; both THWN and XHHW are typically installed in conduit. [D]: While ampacity may differ by size, the advantage isn't a blanket 25% increase; it stems from better thermal properties.
questions.explanation: Incorrectly suggests cost and weight advantages, when XHHW is actually more expensive than THWN. Confuses installation method; both THWN and XHHW are typically installed in conduit. While ampacity may differ by size, the advantage isn't a blanket 25% increase; it stems from better thermal properties. XHHW uses cross-linked polyethylene insulation, providing superior durability and thermal stability compared to THWN's thermoplastic coating. This makes XHHW preferred for main feeders and high-load circuits that generate sustained heat. XHHW's cross-linked polyethylene provides superior insulation durability, preferred for feeders and heavy-load circuits.
